source.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating and Explaining Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
source.authors: Ekagra Gupta; Raj Saha; Aniekan-abasi Inyang; Adam Al Gharib

record.tranche_reason: The study applies a difference-in-means refusal direction and tests ablation and activation addition on new model architectures, directly reproducing the original intervention in text refusal settings.
record.gate_note: The study also reports text-to-tool refusal divergence and system-prompt effects. Those behavioral results do not test whether the refusal direction causes those outcomes; mechanistic rows below cover the direction interventions, patching, prediction, suppression, and the direction-alignment analysis.
record.test_reason: The study extracts a difference-in-means (harmful minus benign) direction at the decision token and reports refusal rates after directional ablation and activation addition in five new instruct models (Table 3). That repeats the original's method and measure. It also extends this to tool-call safety through projection patching and steering, a new setting for V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim to reproduce Arditi et al. on every architecture, saying ablation sharply cuts refusal and addition induces over-refusal 'across every model'. Their own Llama numbers (73→61; 1→1) contradict this. They conclude that text refusal does not transfer to tool calls. They attribute this to suppression of a shared refusal direction plus tool use itself. They call the direction a useful monitor but a blunt control lever.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means direction and tests ablation and activation addition, but selects a model-specific operating layer and studies tool-context activation patching as well. The text states ablation at each layer but does not state that every position is ablated.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported activation suppression differs by model: it is described as significant in four models and null in Llama-3.1-70B. The benign over-refusal effect of addition also varies substantially by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Low refusal-direction activation predicts unsafe tool calls, with ROC AUC 0.689–0.881 across the five models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction activation is a predictive monitor of unsafe tool calls.

fits_no_version.finding: Tool-enabled context lowers refusal-direction activation relative to no-tool chat in four models (t=4.0–9.7). Llama-3.1-70B shows no suppression (t=0.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tool affordance suppresses the refusal signal in a model-dependent way.

fits_no_version.finding: Directions derived from text and from tool contexts are reported as aligned: tools shrink the signal along a shared axis rather than rotating it. No cosine values are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction is shared between chat and tool-call contexts.

record.peer_reviewed: Published at COLM 2026 Workshop on Agent Behavior
record.problems: No control direction is reported for the interventions. The study does not evaluate broad general capabilities, so preservation of other abilities is untested. Suppression statistics use n=96; uncertainty is not reported for the refusal-rate interventions or patching percentages. Tool-call safety is scored with deterministic predicates, which the authors note can miss fabricated authorization values. The remaining failure after patching is not attributed to a tested mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No mechanistic results left out. Behavioral refusal rates, unsafe-tool rates, conditioned-divergence values (Table 1), and system-condition divergence values (Table 2) were not entered as rows because they do not apply, remove, add, or measure the refusal direction, and the listed claim versions do not directly assert text-to-tool divergence.

untested.parts: Preservation of general capabilities after ablation or addition: no capability benchmark is reported. Whether ablation covers every token position is not stated.
No analysis of jailbreak mechanisms or of adversarial training against ablation. The stress mode is not analysed mechanistically.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction geometry. The authors only speculate that additional directions may explain the unrecovered patching share.
No separate probe of a harmfulness judgment, such as at a different token position. The alignment check (R26) gives no numbers and cannot separate the two.
Directions are extracted per model. Transfer across languages, across model variants, or from base to instruct models is not tested.
No comparison of training methods or training stages.
Only no-think inference is used; reasoning before answering is not tested.

missing.what: Steering trade-off in the tool setting. Raising the addition coefficient drives unsafe calls toward zero, but for Qwen removing them costs about 70% benign over-refusal.
missing.locator: Section 5, 'Steering is a blunt lever'; Figure 3

missing.what: Cosine similarity between text-derived and tool-derived directions. The text claims they are aligned, but no values are reported.
Addition coefficients span about 29 (Mistral) to about 75,000 (Gemma), scaled to each model's harm/benign projection gap. This is relevant to the method-sensitivity of the addition rows.

record.verdict_notes: V4 and V5 links were removed or downgraded. The patching rows test V1's mediation in a tool setting, and the authors explicitly leave the cause of the unrecovered share open. The V5 alignment check gives no numbers and cannot separate harmfulness from refusal. The Table 3 ablation baselines are unexplained relative to Table 1. There is no random-direction control and no capability check. This is a workshop paper.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests harmful-prompt refusal ablation and benign-prompt over-refusal from activation addition, but not broad preservation of general capabilities. Its ablation is described as removing the direction at each layer; testing every position is not stated.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment is reported.
The study does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.

Patching tests whether restoring the one-dimensional signal suffices for tool-call safety, but the study does not directly test affine or cone geometry, nor does it establish that additional directions explain the unrecovered portion.
The study compares a harmful-minus-benign direction with a refused-versus-complied direction for harmful prompts; it does not separately probe a harmfulness judgment.
Directions are extracted separately for each model. Cross-language transfer, transferring one model's direction to another model, and transfer from base to instruct models are not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or training stages is reported.
Reasoning-before-answer behavior is not tested; the appendix describes inference as no-think.

rows.check: Relink from V4 to V1. Patching the one-dimensional projection back to its no-tool value is a test of whether the direction mediates refusal in the tool setting. The authors explicitly decline to attribute the unrecovered share to extra directions, citing other layers, positions, nonlinear effects or the affordance/wording confound. So it cannot speak to V4's geometry. Baseline is the set of unsafe calls, so the value is a recovery fraction.

rows.value: reported as aligned; cosine values not stated
rows.locator: Section 3.7, Robustness of the direction; Section 5
rows.note: The authors say the comparison confirms that harmfulness and refusal occupy the same direction, rather than separate directions.
rows.check: No cosine values are given. Both directions come from the same decision token. The harmful-minus-benign direction already mixes harmfulness with refusal, because harmful prompts are mostly refused, so alignment with a refused-minus-complied direction is expected either way. The measure therefore cannot show whether harmfulness is encoded separately. 'Reversed' is not supported.

relation.reason: The study reports its own ablation, addition and patching results on the direction's causal role (Table 3).

tranche.reason: Same harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means direction, ablation at each layer and activation addition, scored by refusal rate (Table 3). This matches the original's method and measure. The differences are a max-norm layer pick in the 35–85% depth band and a regex plus Claude Haiku judge. The tool-call patching adds a T3-style extension.

source_check.notes: The pack lists four verdicts without [lN] ids, so label_id gives their order of listing (unlisted_1–4). The text does not state the ablation/addition prompt n, the Table 3 addition coefficient, the patching layer or tool mode, any random-direction control, or any capability check. The Table 3 baselines (e.g. Gemma 21%) do not match the Table 1 no-tool refusal (0.70–0.86). The paper claims harm and refusal directions coincide and that text- and tool-derived directions are aligned (bears on V5), but gives no cosine values; the alignment is cited to 'Table 3', which holds none.
